content: Reduced levels of circulating estrogen during menopause can lead to symptoms that significantly impact the health and quality of life of women. Hormone therapy, which includes either unopposed estrogen or a combination of estrogen and progestogen, is an effective treatment for these symptoms. However, it is associated with potential risks. Current guidelines recommend using the lowest effective dose of hormone therapy and regularly reviewing the treatment to minimize harm. The purpose of this review was to determine the minimum dose of progestogen that needs to be added to estrogen therapy to prevent an increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia compared to placebo. Endometrial hyperplasia is a condition characterized by the thickening of the uterine lining, which can increase the risk of endometrial carcinoma. The review aimed to evaluate which hormone therapy regimens effectively protect against the development of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, covering studies published up to January 2012. Additional efforts were made to identify relevant trials from citation lists and unpublished data from pharmaceutical companies. The selection criteria for the review included randomized trials comparing unopposed estrogen therapy, continuous combined estrogen-progestogen therapy, and sequential estrogen-progestogen therapy with each other or placebo. These therapies had to be administered for a minimum of 12 months, and the incidence of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, confirmed by biopsy at the end of treatment, was a required outcome. Data on adherence to therapy, rates of additional interventions, and withdrawals due to adverse events were also collected. In this updated review, 46 studies were included. Odds ratios (ORs) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes. However, due to the small number of studies in each comparison and clinical heterogeneity, meta-analysis was not feasible for many outcomes. The main findings revealed that unopposed estrogen therapy is associated with an increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia, regardless of the dose or duration of therapy (ranging from one to three years). For women with an intact uterus, the risk of endometrial hyperplasia was not significantly different from placebo when low-dose estrogen was continuously combined with at least 1 mg of norethisterone acetate (NETA) or 1.5 mg of medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) for two years. Specifically, the odds ratio for 1 mg NETA was 0.04 (95% confidence interval: 0 to 2.8), and no cases of hyperplasia were reported with 1.5 mg MPA. The authors concluded that hormone therapy for postmenopausal women with an intact uterus should include both estrogen and progestogen to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia.
